There's a particular pleasure in noticing things that weren't hidden, exactly—just unattended. The way morning light makes dust visible, turning air into something with substance. The fact that shadows are blue, not gray; look at snow on a sunny day and you'll see it. The way pigeons bob their heads because their eyes can't move much, so they throw their skulls forward to hold the world still.

Attention is a strange gift. It costs nothing and transforms whatever it touches. A tree you've walked past a hundred times becomes particular the moment you actually look: the slight lean of its trunk, the bark splitting like dried clay, the leaves shivering in unison when wind arrives. Even your own street keeps offering details you've never catalogued—a crack shaped like a river delta, a door painted a color no one else chose.

I suspect this is what artists and scientists share, more than talent: a refusal to stop at *just*. Just a tree. Just a shadow. Just a pigeon. The word "just" is where curiosity goes to die. Everything, examined closely enough, turns elaborate. A drop of pond water holds a metropolis. The word "nice" wandered through seven centuries, from foolish to fussy to kind. Maybe children ask better questions because nothing has been filed under "just" yet.

Wonder, then, isn't something you feel. It's something you practice. The world doesn't withhold itself. It sits there, patient and intricate, waiting only for someone to look a little longer than habit requires.
